title: How wine gets its taste
intro: A short guide to the main reasons wines taste different. Each section links to profiles in the atlas where you can see the effect in the scores.

sections.heading: Reading the scores
body: Every profile scores eight traits from 0 to 5. Alcohol and sweetness use fixed real-world anchors so they mean the same thing everywhere in the atlas.
Alcohol: 0 is under about 6% ABV, 1 about 8.5%, 2 about 10.5%, 3 about 12.5%, 4 about 13.75% and 5 is 15% or more (including fortified wines).
Sweetness: 0 bone dry, 1 dry (including Brut sparkling), 2 off-dry, 3 medium-sweet, 4 sweet, 5 lusciously sweet.
Body, acidity, tannin, fruit, oak and earth are relative scores across the wines in the atlas. They describe a typical example; producers and vintages vary.

examples.label: Light and low in alcohol: Mosel Riesling
Full and high in alcohol: Barossa Shiraz

sections.heading: Climate: ripeness versus freshness
body: Sunshine and warmth ripen grapes. Riper grapes have more sugar, which fermentation turns into more alcohol and a fuller body, and their fruit tastes darker and sweeter. At the same time, acidity falls as grapes ripen.
Cooler places keep more acidity and give lighter, more tart-fruited wines with less alcohol. The same grape can taste very different on either side of that line.

sections.heading: Warm days, cold nights
body: Many high-altitude and desert regions have a large difference between day and night temperatures. Warm days build sugar and flavour; cold nights slow the loss of acidity. The result is ripe fruit that still tastes fresh.

sections.heading: The grape sets the frame
body: Each grape brings its own range. Thick-skinned grapes such as Tannat give deep colour and lots of tannin. Nebbiolo is pale yet very tannic, so colour is not a reliable guide to structure.

Aromatic grapes such as Gewürztraminer, Muscat, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc carry high levels of aroma compounds, so they smell strongly of flowers, lychee, citrus or grass even without oak or age. Some grapes, such as Furmint and Assyrtiko, keep high acidity even in warm places.

sections.heading: Fermentation: how dry or sweet a wine ends up
body: Yeast turns grape sugar into alcohol. When fermentation runs to the end, the wine is dry. If it is stopped early, some sugar stays: Moscato d'Asti is stopped at around 5% alcohol, so it is sweet and light.

Port is sweet for a different reason: grape spirit is added during fermentation, which stops the yeast and raises alcohol to around 20% while leaving natural sugar behind. Noble rot (botrytis) concentrates sugar in the grapes themselves, as in Sauternes and Tokaji Aszú.

sections.heading: Skins: red, rosé, white and orange
body: Almost all grape juice is clear. Colour and tannin come from the skins, so what matters is how long the juice stays in contact with them.

Red wine ferments with the skins. Rosé gets only a few hours of contact. White wine is pressed straight away, which is why red grapes can make white sparkling wine (blanc de noirs). Orange or amber wine is white grapes fermented on their skins, which adds colour, tannin and tea-like flavours.

examples.label: White from red grapes: blanc de noirs

sections.heading: Oak and other vessels
body: New, small oak barrels add flavours such as vanilla, toast, cedar and cocoa; American oak often adds coconut and dill. Barrels also let in small amounts of oxygen, which softens tannin over time.
Older or larger barrels add little flavour, and stainless steel adds none, so they keep the focus on fruit. Clay vessels such as qvevri and amphorae give oxygen exchange without oak flavour.

sections.heading: Softer, creamier whites: malolactic and lees
body: Malolactic fermentation converts sharp malic acid (as in green apples) into softer lactic acid. It is normal for red wines; in whites such as Chardonnay it is a choice that can add a buttery note.
Lees are the spent yeast cells left after fermentation. Leaving wine on them adds texture and bread or biscuit aromas, which is central to Champagne.

sections.heading: Where bubbles come from
body: Sparkling wine gets its bubbles from a second fermentation in a closed container, which traps the carbon dioxide. In the traditional method (Champagne, Cava, Crémant) this happens in each bottle, and long contact with the lees adds toasty, bready notes.
In the tank method (Prosecco) it happens in a large pressurised tank, which keeps the wine fresher and more fruit-led.

sections.heading: Ageing: from fruit to savoury
body: Young wines taste of fresh fruit and flowers (primary aromas) and of winemaking such as oak or lees (secondary). With years in bottle, fruit fades and dried-fruit, leather, forest-floor, nutty or honeyed notes appear (tertiary aromas). Tannins soften as they slowly bind together and drop out as sediment.
Only some wines improve this way; most are best young. Profiles with a maturity section show how a specific wine typically develops.

sections.heading: What 'minerality' does and doesn't mean
body: Vines do not pass the taste of rocks into wine. Soil matters through drainage, water supply, heat and how vigorously the vine grows, which affect ripeness and concentration.
Words such as chalk, flint, slate or saline are tasting descriptors for a sensation, often linked to high acidity and restrained fruit. The atlas uses them that way.
